studies.title: Every Creature Has Its Portion
studies.meaning: The claim is universal and it is phrased as an undertaking: there is no moving creature whose provision is not upon God. The commentators are careful that the wording does not make God a debtor; it describes a responsibility He has assumed. Two further things are known, where the creature settles and where it is deposited, and the classical readings differ over whether these mean life and death, the womb and the grave, or simply dwelling and lodging.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the opening of a surah that will spend most of its length on communities destroyed for refusing their prophets. This ayah stands before all of that, and the commentators note the placement: a statement about provision for every creature is set at the head of a surah about collapse. The audience included people whose objection to the message was what following it would cost them.

keyTerms.note: What is given for sustenance rather than what is earned. The pronoun attaches it to the creature, so each has a portion described as already assigned to it rather than as a share of a common supply.
A noun of place from the verb to settle. Commentators read it as where a creature lives, and also as the womb, so the word covers both a lifetime's ground and the first one it occupied.
From the verb to entrust something for safekeeping. It suggests a temporary holding rather than a home, which is why the classical readings of it include the grave.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Anxiety about provision was seasonal and concrete. Rain arriving late meant thin animals and a hungry winter, and everyone had watched a family slide from sufficiency to dependence in a single bad year. Wild animals were observed closely by people who lived alongside them, and the fact that creatures with no stores and no plans were nonetheless fed was an observation available to anyone outdoors.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a moving creature appears here and in an ayah at 6:38 with a strikingly similar structure, each making a universal claim about animals. One says they are communities like you; this one says their provision has been undertaken. Read together, the two give the animal world a standing and a guarantee in almost identical grammar.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Provision is described as an undertaking rather than a distribution, which changes the anxiety it addresses. The question is not whether enough exists but whether anyone has assumed responsibility for it, and the answer is given before any human being is mentioned in the surah. Including every creature makes the claim testable by observation. The closing reference to a clear record ties provision to knowledge rather than to chance.

crossReferences.why: Points at creatures that carry no provision with them and are fed regardless.
Places provision in the heaven, along with what is being promised.
Makes the parallel claim about animals, calling them communities like your own.

studies.applyIt: Name the specific figure or the specific month that your anxiety about money actually attaches to. Write it down. Then notice that the ayah does not promise abundance; it names a responsibility that has been assumed, and the difference between those two is most of what makes the anxiety loud.

studies.title: I Want Nothing But Repair
studies.meaning: This is Shu'ayb's answer to a community that told him to stop interfering with their trade. He does not argue about the practices. He puts a question about his own position, claims clear evidence and honest livelihood, then makes a specific promise: he does not intend to do privately what he tells others not to do. The aim he names is repair, limited to what he can manage, and the speech ends by handing the outcome over.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, inside a sequence of prophets told one after another in this surah. Shu'ayb is sent to the people of Madyan, a trading community on the caravan route north, and the dispute concerns short measures and interference with what people did with their own property. The commentators treat the exchange as the surah's most detailed account of an argument about commerce rather than about worship alone.

keyTerms.note: Something that makes a matter plain, from a root for separating and clarifying. It names a basis he claims to be standing on rather than a wonder he is offering to perform for them.
From the verb to mend what is broken, used of reconciling people and of restoring a thing to working order. It is the exact opposite of the word the Quran uses for corruption in the land.
From a root for agreement and for things fitting together. It names success as a match between a person's effort and what God allows, which is why it cannot be claimed as an achievement.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Madyan sat on the trade route between Arabia and Syria, and its wealth came from handling other people's goods. Measures and weights were the instruments of that business, and a merchant with a shaved weight could take a fraction from every transaction for years without being caught. The community's objection was that a religious teacher had opinions about the scales.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause in which he says he does not want to do himself what he tells others to avoid is unusual in the Quran, where prophets rarely defend their own conduct. Classical commentators note that the accusation being answered is hypocrisy rather than error, and that he meets it with a statement of intention rather than with evidence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets out what a person calling others to change may claim and what they may not. Evidence and honest provision are claimed; results are not. Limiting the aim to what he is able to do removes the pretension from reform, and handing success over to God removes the credit for it. Between them those two clauses describe a way of trying to improve things that does not depend on succeeding.

crossReferences.why: States plainly how hateful it is to say what you do not do.
Gives the instruction about full measure that this speech is defending.
Asks whether people enjoin righteousness on others and forget themselves.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you have advised someone else to do in the last month and check whether you are doing it. If not, either do it this week or stop giving the advice. Shu'ayb answers a charge of hypocrisy by naming his intention, and the only way to keep that claim honest is to check it against something specific.

studies.title: Be Upright As Commanded
studies.meaning: The command is to stand straight, and two qualifications are attached at once. It is to be done as you were commanded, which fixes the standard outside the person, and it takes in those who turned back alongside him. Then a prohibition against going beyond, which the commentators read as the particular danger of uprightness, since somebody correcting their course tends to overcorrect. The closing clause is about being seen rather than about reward.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, near the end of a surah that has recounted one destroyed community after another and the prophets sent to warn them. After all that history the instruction turns personal. Classical sources preserve a report that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) found this ayah among the most demanding addressed to him, and the commentators return to it when discussing what uprightness costs.

keyTerms.note: A form of the verb to stand that means holding a straight line, used of a road without bends. It asks for a direction maintained over time rather than for a single correct act.
From a root for water rising past its banks and for tyranny. It names going beyond a boundary, and its use here warns that zeal has the same shape as the flood it means to prevent.
The same verb used of repentance throughout the Quran. Describing the community as those who turned back with him defines them by a movement they made rather than by a status they hold.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Desert travel depended on holding a line. A caravan that drifted a few degrees off course over a day's march could miss a well by miles, and guides were valued for keeping direction across ground with no landmarks at all. Correction was constant and small. The vocabulary of staying straight was practical language about survival long before it was ever moral language.
studies.didYouKnow: The command in this ayah is singular and the prohibition that follows is plural, which the classical grammarians point out. One man is told to stand straight, and then a whole group is told not to overstep, so the sentence moves from an individual instruction to a communal warning inside a single line.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Uprightness is defined by an external standard rather than by sincerity, which is the work the phrase about being commanded does. That prevents the straight path from becoming whatever a person's own conscience produces. The warning against excess then guards the other flank, since the danger to someone trying to be upright is not usually laxity but zeal. And the sentence closes with seeing rather than with threat.

crossReferences.why: Describes what comes to those who said our Lord is God and then stood straight.
Gives the same command with an instruction not to follow their desires.
Follows immediately, warning against inclining towards those who do wrong.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you have been doing well recently and check it for overcorrection: the early night that became a rule you enforce on everyone, the budget that has made you tight rather than careful. The ayah puts its warning about excess directly after the command to be straight, and it does so for a reason.

studies.title: At Both Ends Of The Day
studies.meaning: Times are given rather than a number: the two ends of the day, and the stretches of night that draw near to them. Then a statement about how good deeds work on bad ones, using a verb for taking something away. The commentators read the prayer named just before as the leading instance of that. The passage closes with patience and a promise that no reward for doing well is lost, so the sequence runs from a fixed practice to a long endurance.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing a surah full of communities that were destroyed. The instruction arrives immediately after that recital of endings, which the commentators read as deliberate: the response to a long account of collapse is a timetable. A widely reported occasion connects the ayah with a man who came to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) after doing something he regretted, and was told this.

keyTerms.note: A dual form for the two edges of something. Naming the day by its ends rather than by hours gives times anyone can find without an instrument, at the boundaries where the light changes.
From a root for approaching and for closeness. It names the parts of the night nearest to the day, so the times given cluster around the transitions rather than around the middle of anything.
A causative verb meaning to make something go. The good deeds are its subject and the bad ones its object, so the removal is described as an action the deeds themselves perform.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Time in Arabia was told by light. Work began when a white thread could be told from a black one and ended when the sun went down; travellers timed departures by first light and rested at midday. Nobody owned a clock. Fixing devotion to the edges of daylight tied it to the two moments everyone in a settlement already noticed and organised their day around.
studies.didYouKnow: The statement that good deeds take away bad ones is among the most quoted half-sentences in the Quran, and in the Arabic the verb has the good deeds acting on the bad rather than a person acting on either. The grammar keeps the agency with the deeds, which classical commentators point out when discussing how the removal is understood.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Regret is given something to do. Instead of prescribing an emotional state the passage supplies a schedule, and it places that schedule at the boundaries of a day so that the whole day sits between two fixed points. The claim about good deeds then explains why the schedule matters, and the closing instruction to be patient adds the missing dimension: this works over a length of time rather than in a moment.

crossReferences.why: Fixes prayer to the sun's decline and the dawn, adding a portion of the night.
Gives similar times, before sunrise and before setting and during the night.
Describes those who are patient and establish prayer as repelling evil with good.

studies.applyIt: Choose one of the two edges of the day, morning or evening, and put a small fixed act there for a week: two minutes of recitation, one page, a set of words you say. Not both ends, one. The ayah anchors devotion to a boundary that arrives whether or not you are ready, and that is the useful part of it.
